subject: physics
title: Heat engines and the second law
key_idea: A heat engine turns some of the heat from a hot source into work and must reject the rest to a cold sink. Indicator diagrams let us find an engine's power and efficiency. The second law sets a maximum efficiency that depends only on the two temperatures.

blocks.text: Both engines run a four-stroke cycle in each cylinder. This section covers the strokes and the diagrams that describe them.

diagram.alt: A sequencing activity. Put the four strokes of a four-stroke engine cycle in the correct order.
diagram.prompt: Put the four strokes in order.
steps: Induction: the piston moves down and draws the mixture or air in.
Compression: the piston moves up and compresses the gas.
Power: the burning gas expands and pushes the piston down.
Exhaust: the piston moves up and pushes the burnt gas out.

items: **Petrol engine:** a mixture of air and fuel is compressed, then a spark ignites it.
**Diesel engine:** only air is compressed, to a much higher pressure. Fuel is injected into the hot air and ignites without a spark.

items.meaning: An idealised cycle made of adiabatic, constant-volume and constant-pressure lines with sharp corners.
A p–V graph measured on a real engine. It is a rounded loop.

items: The real indicator diagram has rounded corners and a smaller loop than the theoretical one.
The reasons include heat lost to the cylinder walls, the valves opening and closing over a period of time, and burning that is not instant.
The area of the loop is the work done by the gas in one cycle.
Induction, compression, power, exhaust.
A diesel engine ignites by compression, a petrol engine by a spark.
The indicator diagram of a real engine is smaller and rounder than the theoretical one.

sections.heading: Power and efficiency of an engine

blocks.text: The indicator diagram gives the power the gas produces. The shaft gives the power delivered. Their difference is lost to friction.

blocks.label: Input power
blocks.formula: input power = calorific value × fuel flow rate
where: Calorific value = energy released per kg of fuel (J/kg)
Fuel flow rate = mass of fuel used per second (kg/s)

blocks.label: Indicated power
blocks.formula: indicated power = (area of p–V loop) × (cycles per second) × (number of cylinders)
where: Area of loop = work per cycle (J)
A four-stroke cycle takes two turns of the crankshaft, so cycles per second = shaft turns per second ÷ 2.

blocks.label: Output or brake power
where: T = torque at the output shaft (N m)
ω = angular speed of the shaft (rad/s)

blocks.label: Friction power
blocks.formula: friction power = indicated power − brake power

blocks.label: Overall efficiency
blocks.formula: overall efficiency = brake power ÷ input power

blocks.label: Thermal efficiency
blocks.formula: thermal efficiency = indicated power ÷ input power

blocks.label: Mechanical efficiency
blocks.formula: mechanical efficiency = brake power ÷ indicated power

items: Thermal efficiency tells you how well the **fuel energy** becomes work in the gas.
Mechanical efficiency tells you how much of that work survives friction in the engine.
Overall efficiency = thermal efficiency × mechanical efficiency.

blocks.text: Questions can use other cycles. They are interpretative and give all the information needed.

items: Indicated power comes from the loop area, the cycle rate and the cylinders.
Brake power is Tω. Friction power is the difference.
Overall = brake ÷ input. Thermal = indicated ÷ input. Mechanical = brake ÷ indicated.

sections.heading: The second law and the limit on efficiency

blocks.text: The first law alone would allow an engine that turns all its heat into work. In practice no such engine exists.

items: An engine that took heat from one reservoir and turned all of it into work obeys the first law, but it is **impossible**.
The **second law** says a heat engine must work between a hot source and a cold sink.
It takes heat Q_H from the source, does work W and rejects heat Q_C to the sink.

blocks.label: Efficiency of a heat engine
where: Q_H = heat taken from the source (J)
Q_C = heat rejected to the sink (J)

diagram.alt: A slider activity. Change the source and sink temperatures and read the maximum theoretical efficiency of an engine.

items: Temperatures must be in **kelvin**.
A hotter source or a colder sink raises the maximum efficiency.
The maximum can never reach 100%, because T_C cannot be zero.
Friction between moving parts wastes work.
Heat is lost through the cylinder walls and in the hot exhaust.
Real processes are not perfectly reversible, and combustion may be incomplete.
The gas does not follow the ideal cycle exactly.

blocks.text: Combined heat and power schemes use the heat rejected to the sink, for example to heat buildings. This makes use of both W and Q_H.

items: A heat engine needs a source and a sink, and must reject heat.
Maximum efficiency = (T_H − T_C) ÷ T_H, in kelvin.
Real engines fall short because of friction and heat losses.

blocks.text: A reversed heat engine uses work to move heat from cold to hot. The same principle drives refrigerators and heat pumps.

items: A **refrigerator** takes heat Q_C from a cold space and rejects Q_H to the warmer room. Its purpose is to cool the cold space.
A **heat pump** moves heat from the cold outside to the warm inside. Its purpose is to heat the warm space.
Work W is put in, so Q_H = Q_C + W.

blocks.label: Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator
blocks.formula: COP_ref = Q_C ÷ W = Q_C ÷ (Q_H − Q_C) = T_C ÷ (T_H − T_C)

blocks.label: Coefficient of performance of a heat pump
blocks.formula: COPₕₚ = Q_H ÷ W = Q_H ÷ (Q_H − Q_C) = T_H ÷ (T_H − T_C)

items: The temperature forms of the COP give the **maximum** values.
COP is not limited to 1: a good heat pump delivers several joules of heat for each joule of work.
The smaller the temperature difference, the larger the COP.
Reversed engines move heat from cold to hot using work.
COP of a refrigerator is Q_C ÷ W. COP of a heat pump is Q_H ÷ W.
A smaller temperature difference gives a higher COP.

checks.q: An engine uses fuel of calorific value 4.4 × 10⁷ J/kg at 2.0 × 10⁻³ kg/s. Its indicated power is 30 kW and its brake power is 24 kW. Calculate its thermal, mechanical and overall efficiencies.
A heat engine takes in heat from a source at 900 K and rejects heat to a sink at 300 K. Calculate its maximum theoretical efficiency.
A heat pump delivers 3.0 kJ of heat to a room for every 1.0 kJ of work supplied. Calculate its coefficient of performance and the heat it takes from outside.
